name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q01 - General electronic configuration of s-block elements

questiontext.text: What are the general valence shell electronic configurations of alkali metals (Group 1) and alkaline earth metals (Group 2), respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The s-block elements are those in which the last electron enters the outermost \(s\)-orbital, which can accommodate a maximum of two electrons.

Step 2: Analysis
Group 1 elements (alkali metals) have one valence electron in their outermost \(s\)-orbital outside a noble gas core, giving \([\text{noble gas}]ns^1\). Group 2 elements (alkaline earth metals) have two valence electrons in their outermost \(s\)-orbital, giving \([\text{noble gas}]ns^2\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The general electronic configurations are \([\text{noble gas}]ns^1\) for alkali metals and \([\text{noble gas}]ns^2\) for alkaline earth metals.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q02 - Half-life of longest-lived isotope of francium

questiontext.text: Francium is a highly radioactive alkali metal. What is the half-life of its longest-lived isotope, \(^{223}\mathrm{Fr}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Among the Group 1 alkali metals, francium (\(Z=87\)) is highly radioactive and occurs only in trace amounts (\(\sim 10^{-18}\text{ ppm}\)) in the lithosphere.

Step 2: Fact Retrieval
The longest-lived isotope of francium is \(^{223}\mathrm{Fr}\), which has a half-life of only \(21\text{ minutes}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The half-life of \(^{223}\mathrm{Fr}\) is \(21\text{ minutes}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q03 - Abundance of Group 2 elements in earth crust

questiontext.text: Which pair of Group 2 elements ranks fifth and sixth in abundance, respectively, in the Earth's crust?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Alkaline earth metals vary widely in their natural abundance in the Earth's crust.

Step 2: Fact Retrieval
Calcium and magnesium rank fifth and sixth in abundance respectively in the Earth's crust (\(4.6\%\) and \(2.76\%\) by weight in the lithosphere). Strontium and barium have much lower abundances, beryllium is rare, and radium is the rarest.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Calcium and magnesium rank fifth and sixth in abundance respectively.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q04 - Hydration enthalpy order of alkali metal ions

questiontext.text: Which of the following represents the correct decreasing order of hydration enthalpies of alkali metal ions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Hydration enthalpy of an ion depends on its charge density; for ions of the same charge (\(+1\)), smaller ionic radius leads to stronger electrostatic attraction with water molecules and thus a larger magnitude of hydration enthalpy.

Step 2: Trend Analysis
Since ionic radius increases down Group 1 from \(\mathrm{Li}^+\) (\(76\text{ pm}\)) to \(\mathrm{Cs}^+\) (\(167\text{ pm}\)), hydration enthalpy decreases down the group: \(\mathrm{Li}^+ > \mathrm{Na}^+ > \mathrm{K}^+ > \mathrm{Rb}^+ > \mathrm{Cs}^+\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The decreasing order of hydration enthalpies is \(\mathrm{Li}^+ > \mathrm{Na}^+ > \mathrm{K}^+ > \mathrm{Rb}^+ > \mathrm{Cs}^+\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q05 - Alkali metal with the lowest melting point

questiontext.text: Which of the following alkali metals has the lowest melting point?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Alkali metals have weak metallic bonding due to the presence of only a single valence electron. As atomic size increases down Group 1, the metallic bond weakens further, causing melting points to decrease.

Step 2: Data Comparison
The melting points of \(\mathrm{Na}\), \(\mathrm{K}\), \(\mathrm{Rb}\), and \(\mathrm{Cs}\) are \(371\text{ K}\), \(336\text{ K}\), \(312\text{ K}\), and \(302\text{ K}\), respectively.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Caesium (\(\mathrm{Cs}\)) has the lowest melting point (\(302\text{ K}\)) among these alkali metals.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q06 - Alkali metals used in photoelectric cells

questiontext.text: Which pair of alkali metals is most useful as electrodes in photoelectric cells because light energy can easily eject electrons from their atoms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
When an alkali metal is irradiated with light, the absorbed light energy can be sufficient to make an atom lose an electron if its ionisation enthalpy is sufficiently low.

Step 2: Application
Because of their low ionisation enthalpies, potassium (\(\mathrm{K}\)) and caesium (\(\mathrm{Cs}\)) readily emit electrons upon irradiation and are therefore useful as electrodes in photoelectric cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Caesium and potassium are used as electrodes in photoelectric cells.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q07 - Oxidation state of potassium in KO2

questiontext.text: What is the oxidation state of potassium in potassium superoxide (\(\mathrm{KO}_2\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The compound is neutral potassium superoxide, \(\mathrm{KO}_2\).

Step 2: Conceptual Principle and Working
The superoxide species is \(\mathrm{O}_2^-\), which carries a net charge of \(-1\) (each oxygen atom has an oxidation state of \(-\frac{1}{2}\)). Since \(\mathrm{KO}_2\) is electrically neutral, let \(x\) be the oxidation state of \(\mathrm{K}\):
\[x + (-1) = 0 \implies x = +1\]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The oxidation state of potassium in \(\mathrm{KO}_2\) is \(+1\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q08 - Storage of alkali metals in kerosene oil

questiontext.text: Why are alkali metals normally stored in kerosene oil?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Alkali metals have large atomic sizes and low ionisation enthalpies, making them highly reactive.

Step 2: Analysis
They tarnish in dry air due to oxide formation and react vigorously with moisture/water to form hydroxides and dihydrogen. Keeping them immersed in kerosene oil prevents contact with air and moisture.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Alkali metals are kept in kerosene oil because of their high reactivity towards air and water.

answer.text: To prevent them from subliming at room temperature
Because they are soluble in kerosene oil
Because of their high reactivity towards air and water

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q09 - Colour and magnetic property of alkali metal superoxides

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly describes the colour and magnetic nature of pure alkali metal superoxides (\(\mathrm{MO}_2\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Pure alkali metal oxides (\(\mathrm{M}_2\mathrm{O}\)) and peroxides (\(\mathrm{M}_2\mathrm{O}_2\)) are colourless and diamagnetic, whereas superoxides (\(\mathrm{MO}_2\)) contain the \(\mathrm{O}_2^-\) ion.

Step 2: Analysis
The \(\mathrm{O}_2^-\) ion has one unpaired electron in a \(\pi^*2p\) molecular orbital, making superoxides paramagnetic. Physically, superoxides are yellow or orange in colour.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pure alkali metal superoxides are yellow or orange in colour and paramagnetic.

answer.text: Yellow or orange in colour and paramagnetic

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q10 - Melting and boiling point trend of alkali metal halides

questiontext.text: For a given alkali metal \(\mathrm{M}\), what is the correct decreasing order of melting and boiling points of its halides \(\mathrm{MX}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
All alkali metal halides (\(\mathrm{MX}\)) are high-melting crystalline solids whose melting and boiling points depend on lattice strength.

Step 2: Trend Analysis
As the size of the halide ion increases from \(\mathrm{F}^-\) to \(\mathrm{I}^-\), the inter-ionic distance increases and the lattice enthalpy decreases. Consequently, the melting and boiling points always follow the trend: fluoride > chloride > bromide > iodide.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct decreasing order is \(\mathrm{MF} > \mathrm{MCl} > \mathrm{MBr} > \mathrm{MI}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q11 - Baking soda decomposition and use

questiontext.text: Sodium hydrogencarbonate (\(\mathrm{NaHCO}_3\)) is known as baking soda because on heating it decomposes to generate bubbles of which gas, making cakes and pastries light and fluffy?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sodium hydrogencarbonate is thermally unstable and decomposes on heating according to \(2\mathrm{NaHCO}_3 \rightarrow \mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3 + \mathrm{CO}_2 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).

Step 2: Analysis
The evolution of carbon dioxide (\(\mathrm{CO}_2\)) gas bubbles leaves small holes in cakes or pastries, making them light and fluffy. For the same reason, \(\mathrm{NaHCO}_3\) is also used in fire extinguishers.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The gas generated on heating baking soda is carbon dioxide (\(\mathrm{CO}_2\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q12 - Composition and medicinal use of milk of magnesia

questiontext.text: What is "milk of magnesia", commonly used as an antacid in medicine?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Alkaline earth metal hydroxides are sparingly soluble in water and mildly basic.

Step 2: Fact Retrieval
A suspension of magnesium hydroxide (\(\mathrm{Mg(OH)}_2\)) in water is called milk of magnesia and is used as an antacid in medicine (whereas magnesium carbonate is an ingredient of toothpaste).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Milk of magnesia is a suspension of magnesium hydroxide in water.

answer.text: A suspension of calcium hydroxide in water
A paste of magnesium carbonate in ethanol
A suspension of magnesium hydroxide in water

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q13 - Magnesium in chlorophyll

questiontext.text: Which s-block metal is present in chlorophyll, the main pigment for the absorption of light in plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Divalent \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\) and \(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\) ions play vital biological roles in both animals and plants.

Step 2: Fact Retrieval
Chlorophyll, the main pigment responsible for light absorption in plants, contains magnesium (\(\mathrm{Mg}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The s-block metal present in chlorophyll is magnesium.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q14 - Why alkali metals are not found free in nature

questiontext.text: Why are alkali metals never found in the free (uncombined) state in nature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
All alkali metals have a single valence electron, \(ns^1\), outside a noble gas core.

Step 2: Analysis
Because the outermost \(s\)-electron is loosely held, alkali metals have very low ionisation enthalpies and are the most electropositive metals. They readily lose this electron to form monovalent \(\mathrm{M}^+\) ions and react rapidly with air and moisture, so they never occur in the free state.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
They are never found free in nature because their loosely held \(ns^1\) electron makes them the most electropositive metals that readily lose an electron to form \(\mathrm{M}^+\) ions.

answer.text: They have very high melting and boiling points
Their loosely held \(ns^1\) electron makes them strongly electropositive, readily forming \(\mathrm{M}^+\) ions
They have high ionisation enthalpies and high densities
They form stable \(M^-\) anions on reaction with water

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q15 - Cause of diagonal relationship in the periodic table

questiontext.text: Lithium shows similarities to magnesium, and beryllium to aluminium, in many of their chemical properties. What is the primary cause of this diagonal relationship?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Moving across a period decreases ionic size and increases charge, whereas moving down a group increases ionic size. Along a diagonal from top-left to bottom-right, these opposing effects largely cancel out.

Step 2: Analysis
Thus, \(\mathrm{Li}^+\) (\(76\text{ pm}\)) and \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\) (\(72\text{ pm}\)) have similar sizes, and \(\mathrm{Be}^{2+}\) (\(31\text{ pm}\)) and \(\mathrm{Al}^{3+}\) have nearly the same charge/radius ratio. This similarity in ionic sizes and/or charge/radius ratio causes the diagonal relationship.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The diagonal relationship is due to similarity in ionic sizes and/or charge/radius ratio of the elements.

answer.text: Presence of vacant \(d\)-orbitals in all four elements
Similarity in ionic sizes and/or charge/radius ratio

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q16 - Reason for decrease in ionization enthalpy down Group 1

questiontext.text: Why do the ionisation enthalpies of alkali metals decrease down Group 1 from \(\mathrm{Li}\) to \(\mathrm{Cs}\) despite the increase in nuclear charge?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ionisation enthalpy depends on the effective nuclear attraction experienced by the outermost valence electron.

Step 2: Analysis
As we move down Group 1 from \(\mathrm{Li}\) to \(\mathrm{Cs}\), new electron shells are added. The effect of increasing atomic size outweighs the increasing nuclear charge, and the outermost \(ns^1\) electron is very well screened from the nuclear charge by inner-shell electrons.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The effect of increasing atomic size and effective screening outweighs the increasing nuclear charge.

answer.text: The number of valence electrons decreases down the group
The hydration enthalpy increases down the group
The metallic bonding becomes stronger down the group
The effect of increasing atomic size and screening outweighs the increasing nuclear charge

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q17 - Density anomaly between sodium and potassium

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements regarding the densities of alkali metals is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Because of their large atomic sizes, alkali metals have low densities, which generally increase down Group 1 from \(\mathrm{Li}\) to \(\mathrm{Cs}\).

Step 2: Data Check
From the physical properties of alkali metals, the densities are: \(\mathrm{Li} = 0.53\text{ g cm}^{-3}\), \(\mathrm{Na} = 0.97\text{ g cm}^{-3}\), \(\mathrm{K} = 0.86\text{ g cm}^{-3}\), \(\mathrm{Rb} = 1.53\text{ g cm}^{-3}\), and \(\mathrm{Cs} = 1.90\text{ g cm}^{-3}\). Thus, potassium is lighter than sodium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Potassium has a lower density than sodium.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q18 - Flame emission wavelengths of alkali metals

questiontext.text: In flame photometry, an alkali metal imparts a yellow colour to an oxidizing flame with an emission wavelength of \(589.2\text{ nm}\). Identify the metal.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each alkali metal emits radiation at a characteristic wavelength in the visible spectrum when heated in an oxidizing flame.

Step 2: Data Identification
The characteristic wavelengths and colours are: \(\mathrm{Li}\) (\(670.8\text{ nm}\), crimson red), \(\mathrm{Na}\) (\(589.2\text{ nm}\), yellow), \(\mathrm{K}\) (\(766.5\text{ nm}\), violet), \(\mathrm{Rb}\) (\(780.0\text{ nm}\), red violet), and \(\mathrm{Cs}\) (\(455.5\text{ nm}\), blue).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The metal emitting yellow light at \(589.2\text{ nm}\) is sodium (\(\mathrm{Na}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q19 - Direct reaction of lithium with nitrogen

questiontext.text: Which alkali metal shows exceptional behaviour by reacting directly with the nitrogen of air to form a nitride?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Due to its exceptionally small size and high lattice energy of the resulting nitride, lithium exhibits anomalous reactivity compared to other Group 1 metals.

Step 2: Analysis
On combustion in air, lithium reacts directly with nitrogen to form lithium nitride, \(\mathrm{Li}_3\mathrm{N}\), in addition to \(\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O}\). Other alkali metals do not form nitrides directly with atmospheric nitrogen.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Lithium is the only alkali metal that reacts directly with nitrogen of air to form a nitride (\(\mathrm{Li}_3\mathrm{N}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q20 - Reaction of alkali metals with dihydrogen

questiontext.text: Alkali metals react with dihydrogen at about \(673\text{ K}\) (and lithium at \(1073\text{ K}\)) to form hydrides. What is the nature of all alkali metal hydrides?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Alkali metals are strongly electropositive and transfer their valence electron to hydrogen when heated with \(\mathrm{H}_2\): \(2\mathrm{M} + \mathrm{H}_2 \rightarrow 2\mathrm{M}^+\mathrm{H}^-\).

Step 2: Analysis
All alkali metal hydrides are ionic solids containing \(\mathrm{M}^+\) and \(\mathrm{H}^-\) ions and possess high melting points.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
All alkali metal hydrides are ionic solids with high melting points.

answer.text: Polymeric covalent solids with low melting points

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q21 - Most covalent lithium halide

questiontext.text: Among the halides of lithium (\(\mathrm{LiF}, \mathrm{LiCl}, \mathrm{LiBr}, \mathrm{LiI}\)), which one is the most covalent in nature and why?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The distortion of the electron cloud of an anion by a cation is called polarisation. Greater polarisation leads to higher covalent character.

Step 2: Analysis
The \(\mathrm{Li}^+\) ion is very small and has a strong tendency to distort the electron cloud of a negative halide ion. Since an anion with a larger size is more easily distorted, \(\mathrm{I}^-\) is polarised to the greatest extent among halides.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Lithium iodide (\(\mathrm{LiI}\)) is the most covalent because the large \(\mathrm{I}^-\) ion is most easily polarised by \(\mathrm{Li}^+\).

answer.text: \(\mathrm{LiI}\), because the large \(\mathrm{I}^-\) ion is most easily distorted by \(\mathrm{Li}^+\)
\(\mathrm{LiF}\), because \(\mathrm{F}^-\) is the most electronegative halide ion
\(\mathrm{LiCl}\), because \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\) has intermediate size and high hydration energy
\(\mathrm{LiBr}\), because \(\mathrm{Br}^-\) has the highest electron affinity

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q22 - Concentrated alkali metal solution in liquid ammonia

questiontext.text: When the concentration of an alkali metal dissolved in liquid ammonia is increased, what changes occur in the colour and magnetic nature of the solution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Dilute solutions of alkali metals in liquid ammonia contain ammoniated electrons, which absorb visible light to impart a deep blue colour and make the solution paramagnetic.

Step 2: Analysis
In a concentrated solution, the blue colour changes to bronze colour and the solution becomes diamagnetic.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The solution changes from deep blue and paramagnetic to bronze-coloured and diamagnetic.

answer.text: It changes to colourless and remains paramagnetic
It changes to bronze colour and becomes diamagnetic
It changes to golden yellow and becomes ferromagnetic
It remains deep blue and becomes diamagnetic

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q23 - Reason for paramagnetism of KO2

questiontext.text: Why is potassium superoxide (\(\mathrm{KO}_2\)) paramagnetic?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Paramagnetism arises from the presence of one or more unpaired electrons in an atom, ion, or molecule.

Step 2: Molecular Orbital Analysis
Potassium superoxide consists of \(\mathrm{K}^+\) and the superoxide ion \(\mathrm{O}_2^-\). While \(\mathrm{K}^+\) has a noble gas core with all electrons paired, the \(\mathrm{O}_2^-\) ion has \(17\) electrons, leaving one unpaired electron in a \(\pi^*2p\) antibonding molecular orbital.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{KO}_2\) is paramagnetic because of one unpaired electron in the \(\pi^*2p\) molecular orbital of \(\mathrm{O}_2^-\).

answer.text: Because \(\mathrm{K}^+\) has an unpaired electron in its \(4s\) orbital
Because \(\mathrm{O}_2^-\) has two unpaired electrons in \(\sigma^*2p\) orbitals
Because \(\mathrm{O}_2^-\) has one unpaired electron in a \(\pi^*2p\) molecular orbital

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q24 - Products of hydrolysis of KO2 with water

questiontext.text: When potassium superoxide (\(\mathrm{KO}_2\)) is hydrolysed by water, which products are formed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Alkali metal superoxides react readily with water in a disproportionation/hydrolysis reaction.

Step 2: Balanced Equation
\[2\mathrm{MO}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{M}^+ + 2\mathrm{OH}^- + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 + \mathrm{O}_2\]
For \(\mathrm{KO}_2\), the products are potassium hydroxide (\(\mathrm{KOH}\)), hydrogen peroxide (\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\)), and dioxygen (\(\mathrm{O}_2\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hydrolysis of \(\mathrm{KO}_2\) produces \(\mathrm{KOH}\), \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\), and \(\mathrm{O}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q25 - Solubility of lithium halides in organic solvents

questiontext.text: Unlike other alkali metal chlorides, lithium chloride (\(\mathrm{LiCl}\)) is soluble in organic solvents such as ethanol, acetone, ethyl acetate, and pyridine. What is the reason for this?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Lithium has an exceptionally small ionic size and a high charge/radius ratio (high polarising power).

Step 2: Analysis
This high polarising power causes increased covalent character in lithium compounds such as \(\mathrm{LiCl}\), which is responsible for their solubility in organic solvents like ethanol, acetone, ethyl acetate, and pyridine.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{LiCl}\) is soluble in organic solvents due to its increased covalent character arising from the high polarising power of \(\mathrm{Li}^+\).

answer.text: Increased covalent character due to the small size and high polarising power of \(\mathrm{Li}^+\)
Very low hydration enthalpy of \(\mathrm{Li}^+\) in water
Purely ionic bonding and very high lattice enthalpy
Formation of stable superoxide complexes with organic solvents

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q26 - Thermal stability of lithium carbonate vs sodium carbonate

questiontext.text: Why does lithium carbonate (\(\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\)) decompose easily at a lower temperature upon heating, whereas sodium carbonate (\(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\)) is thermally stable?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
As electropositive character increases down Group 1, the thermal stability of alkali metal carbonates increases.

Step 2: Analysis
Lithium, being very small in size, strongly polarises the large carbonate ion (\(\mathrm{CO}_3^{2-}\)), distorting its electron cloud and leading to the formation of the more stable oxide \(\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O}\) and \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) upon heating.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The small \(\mathrm{Li}^+\) ion polarises the large \(\mathrm{CO}_3^{2-}\) ion, favouring decomposition into more stable \(\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O}\) and \(\mathrm{CO}_2\).

answer.text: Small \(\mathrm{Li}^+\) polarises the large \(\mathrm{CO}_3^{2-}\) ion, leading to more stable \(\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{O}\) and \(\mathrm{CO}_2\)
\(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\) has a lower lattice enthalpy than \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{O}\)
\(\mathrm{Li}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\) exists only as a decahydrate that melts before decomposing

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q27 - Hydrogencarbonate that does not exist as a solid

questiontext.text: Which of the following alkali metal hydrogencarbonates is NOT obtained in the solid form?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
All alkali metals except lithium form solid hydrogencarbonates (\(\mathrm{MHCO}_3\)).

Step 2: Analysis
Due to the small size and high polarising power of \(\mathrm{Li}^+\), lithium hydrogencarbonate (\(\mathrm{LiHCO}_3\)) does not exist as a solid (similar to magnesium hydrogencarbonate).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{LiHCO}_3\) is not obtained in the solid form.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q28 - Reaction of alkali metals with ethyne

questiontext.text: Which alkali metal forms NO ethynide on reaction with ethyne?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Alkali metals generally react with proton donors such as alcohol, gaseous ammonia, and alkynes (like ethyne).

Step 2: Anomalous Behaviour
Unlike the other alkali metals, lithium forms no ethynide on reaction with ethyne.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Lithium does not form an ethynide on reaction with ethyne.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q29 - By-product of ammonia recovery in Solvay process

questiontext.text: In the Solvay process for the manufacture of sodium carbonate, ammonia (\(\mathrm{NH}_3\)) is recovered by treating \(\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{Cl}\) with \(\mathrm{Ca(OH)}_2\). Which compound is obtained as a by-product in this recovery step?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ammonia is recycled in the Solvay process by reacting the ammonium chloride liquor with slaked lime.

Step 2: Balanced Equation
\[2\mathrm{NH}_4\mathrm{Cl} + \mathrm{Ca(OH)}_2 \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NH}_3 + \mathrm{CaCl}_2 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]
Thus, calcium chloride (\(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\)) is obtained as the by-product.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Calcium chloride (\(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\)) is obtained as a by-product.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q30 - Heating of washing soda above 373 K

questiontext.text: When sodium carbonate decahydrate (\(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\cdot 10\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)) is heated above \(373\text{ K}\), it loses all its water of crystallisation to form a white powder. What is this anhydrous white powder called?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Heating washing soda (\(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\cdot 10\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)) first yields the monohydrate (\(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\cdot \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)) and above \(373\text{ K}\) gives completely anhydrous \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\).

Step 2: Fact Retrieval
Anhydrous sodium carbonate (\(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\)) obtained as a white powder above \(373\text{ K}\) is called soda ash.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The anhydrous white powder is called soda ash.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q31 - Deliquescent impurities in crude sodium chloride

questiontext.text: Crude sodium chloride obtained by crystallisation of brine solution absorbs moisture easily from the atmosphere due to the presence of which deliquescent impurities?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Deliquescent substances absorb moisture readily from the atmosphere and dissolve in it.

Step 2: Analysis
Crude \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) contains \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\), \(\mathrm{CaSO}_4\), \(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\), and \(\mathrm{MgCl}_2\). Specifically, calcium chloride (\(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\)) and magnesium chloride (\(\mathrm{MgCl}_2\)) are deliquescent impurities that absorb moisture from the air.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The deliquescent impurities in crude \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) are \(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\) and \(\mathrm{MgCl}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q32 - Solubility of sodium chloride in water

questiontext.text: What is the solubility of pure sodium chloride (\(\mathrm{NaCl}\)) in \(100\text{ g}\) of water at \(273\text{ K}\), and how does it change with increasing temperature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Fact Retrieval
Sodium chloride melts at \(1081\text{ K}\) and has a solubility of \(36.0\text{ g}\) in \(100\text{ g}\) of water at \(273\text{ K}\).

Step 2: Temperature Dependence
Unlike many other salts, the solubility of \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) in water does not increase appreciably with an increase in temperature.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Its solubility is \(36.0\text{ g}\) per \(100\text{ g}\) of water at \(273\text{ K}\), and it does not increase appreciably with temperature.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q33 - Reaction of sodium hydroxide with atmospheric CO2

Sodium hydroxide is a strong alkali that absorbs moisture from the air (deliquescence) and reacts with acidic oxides such as carbon dioxide.

At the surface, the aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) solution reacts with atmospheric \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) to form sodium carbonate (\(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\)).

The compound formed at the surface is \(\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q34 - ATP consumption by the sodium-potassium pump

A discriminatory active-transport mechanism called the sodium-potassium pump maintains steep concentration gradients of \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) and \(\mathrm{K}^+\) across cell membranes.

Operating this pump consumes more than one-third of the ATP used by a resting animal (about \(15\text{ kg}\) of ATP per \(24\text{ h}\) in a resting human).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q35 - Sodium and potassium concentrations in blood plasma and RBCs

questiontext.text: In human blood, what are the typical concentrations of \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) and \(\mathrm{K}^+\) ions inside red blood cells, as compared to \(143\text{ mmol L}^{-1}\) (\(\mathrm{Na}^+\)) and \(5\text{ mmol L}^{-1}\) (\(\mathrm{K}^+\)) in blood plasma?

The sodium-potassium pump maintains opposite concentration gradients for \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) and \(\mathrm{K}^+\) across cell membranes: \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) is high outside cells, whereas \(\mathrm{K}^+\) is high inside cells.

Step 2: Data Retrieval
In blood plasma, \(\mathrm{Na}^+ = 143\text{ mmol L}^{-1}\) and \(\mathrm{K}^+ = 5\text{ mmol L}^{-1}\). Within red blood cells, these concentrations change to \(10\text{ mmol L}^{-1}\) (\(\mathrm{Na}^+\)) and \(105\text{ mmol L}^{-1}\) (\(\mathrm{K}^+\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Inside red blood cells, the concentrations are \(10\text{ mmol L}^{-1}\) for \(\mathrm{Na}^+\) and \(105\text{ mmol L}^{-1}\) for \(\mathrm{K}^+\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q36 - Comparison of first and second ionization enthalpies of Group 1 and Group 2

questiontext.text: How do the first and second ionisation enthalpies of alkaline earth metals (Group 2) compare with those of the corresponding alkali metals (Group 1) in the same period?

However, removing a second electron from a Group 1 \(\mathrm{M}^+\) ion disrupts a stable noble-gas core, whereas removing a second electron from a Group 2 \(\mathrm{M}^+\) ion (\(ns^1\)) achieves a noble-gas core. Thus, the second ionisation enthalpies of alkaline earth metals are smaller than those of the corresponding alkali metals.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The first ionisation enthalpies of Group 2 metals are higher, while their second ionisation enthalpies are smaller than those of the corresponding Group 1 metals.

The hydration enthalpies of alkaline earth metal ions are larger than those of alkali metal ions.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q38 - Kinetic inertness of beryllium and magnesium to air and water

Although \(\mathrm{Be}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg}\) are thermodynamically reactive metals, their surface chemistry controls their reaction rate with air and water.

Beryllium and magnesium form a protective oxide film on their surface, which renders them kinetically inert to oxygen and water.

They are kinetically inert because of the formation of an oxide film on their surface.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q39 - Preparation of BeF2 and BeCl2

questiontext.text: What is the best route for the preparation of beryllium fluoride (\(\mathrm{BeF}_2\))?

While all alkaline earth metals combine with halogens at elevated temperatures, specific laboratory/preparative routes are preferred for beryllium halides.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q40 - Preparation of beryllium hydride

questiontext.text: Unlike other Group 2 elements, beryllium does not combine directly with hydrogen upon heating. How is \(\mathrm{BeH}_2\) prepared?

All Group 2 elements except beryllium combine directly with hydrogen on heating to form hydrides (\(\mathrm{MH}_2\)).

\(\mathrm{BeH}_2\) is prepared by reacting beryllium chloride with lithium aluminium hydride:

\(\mathrm{BeH}_2\) is prepared by the reaction of \(\mathrm{BeCl}_2\) with \(\mathrm{LiAlH}_4\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q41 - Ammoniates from Group 2 solutions in liquid ammonia

questiontext.text: Alkaline earth metals dissolve in liquid ammonia to give deep blue-black solutions. What is the formula of the ammoniate recovered from these solutions?

From these deep blue-black solutions, the hexammoniates of formula \([\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{NH}_3)_6]^{2+}\) can be recovered.

The ammoniate recovered is \([\mathrm{M}(\mathrm{NH}_3)_6]^{2+}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q42 - Structure and nature of Group 2 monoxides

Alkaline earth metals burn in oxygen to form monoxides (\(\mathrm{MO}\)).

Except for \(\mathrm{BeO}\), all Group 2 monoxides (\(\mathrm{MgO}\), \(\mathrm{CaO}\), \(\mathrm{SrO}\), \(\mathrm{BaO}\)) have the ionic rock-salt structure and are basic. \(\mathrm{BeO}\) is essentially covalent in nature and amphoteric.

\(\mathrm{BeO}\) is essentially covalent and amphoteric.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q43 - Trends in Group 2 hydroxides

questiontext.text: Moving down Group 2 from \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)}_2\) to \(\mathrm{Ba(OH)}_2\), how do the solubility, thermal stability, and basic character of the hydroxides change?

As atomic number increases down Group 2, the cationic size increases and electropositive character increases.

From \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)}_2\) to \(\mathrm{Ba(OH)}_2\), the solubility in water, thermal stability, and basic character of the hydroxides all increase with increasing atomic number (though they remain less basic and less stable than alkali metal hydroxides).

Solubility, thermal stability, and basic character all increase from \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)}_2\) to \(\mathrm{Ba(OH)}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q44 - Amphoteric reactions of beryllium hydroxide

questiontext.text: When beryllium hydroxide (\(\mathrm{Be(OH)}_2\)) dissolves in excess alkali (\(\mathrm{OH}^-\)), what is the formula of the complex ion formed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Beryllium hydroxide is amphoteric and reacts with both acids and alkalies.

With excess hydroxide ions, \(\mathrm{Be(OH)}_2\) forms the tetrahedral beryllate ion:

The complex ion formed is the beryllate ion, \([\mathrm{Be(OH)}_4]^{2-}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q45 - Stability of beryllium carbonate

questiontext.text: Beryllium carbonate (\(\mathrm{BeCO}_3\)) is thermally unstable and decomposes readily. Under what condition can \(\mathrm{BeCO}_3\) be kept without decomposing?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Because \(\mathrm{Be}^{2+}\) is extremely small and strongly polarising, \(\mathrm{BeCO}_3\) readily decomposes to \(\mathrm{BeO}\) and \(\mathrm{CO}_2\): \(\mathrm{BeCO}_3 \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{BeO} + \mathrm{CO}_2\).

Step 2: Equilibrium Principle
Keeping \(\mathrm{BeCO}_3\) in an atmosphere of \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) shifts the decomposition equilibrium backward, preventing its decomposition.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{BeCO}_3\) can be kept only in an atmosphere of \(\mathrm{CO}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q46 - Enthalpy of formation trends of alkali metal halides

\(\Delta_f H^\circ\) values for fluorides become less negative down the group, whereas the reverse is true for chlorides, bromides, and iodides.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q47 - Why lithium is the strongest reducing agent in aqueous solution

questiontext.text: Lithium has the highest first ionisation enthalpy (\(520\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) among all alkali metals, yet it is the strongest reducing agent in aqueous solution (\(E^\circ = -3.04\text{ V}\)). Which factor accounts for this?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The standard electrode potential \(E^\circ\) measures the overall change in aqueous solution:
\[\mathrm{M(s)} \xrightarrow{\Delta_{\text{sub}}H} \mathrm{M(g)} \xrightarrow{\text{IE}} \mathrm{M^+(g)} + \mathrm{e}^- \xrightarrow{\Delta_{\text{hyd}}H} \mathrm{M^+(aq)}\]

Step 2: Thermodynamic Analysis
Although \(\mathrm{Li}\) has the highest ionisation enthalpy in Group 1, the very small \(\mathrm{Li}^+\) ion has the highest hydration enthalpy (\(-506\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)). This large exothermic hydration enthalpy more than compensates for the high ionisation enthalpy, resulting in the most negative \(E^\circ\) (\(-3.04\text{ V}\)) and the highest reducing power.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The highest hydration enthalpy of the small \(\mathrm{Li}^+\) ion accounts for its high negative \(E^\circ\) value and strong reducing power.

answer.text: The highest hydration enthalpy of the small \(\mathrm{Li}^+\) ion

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q48 - Thermal dehydration vs hydrolysis of hydrated Group 2 halides

Small, highly polarising cations (\(\mathrm{Be}^{2+}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\)) polarise coordinated water molecules strongly, causing hydrolysis upon heating rather than simple loss of water.

The dehydration of hydrated chlorides, bromides, and iodides of \(\mathrm{Ca}\), \(\mathrm{Sr}\), and \(\mathrm{Ba}\) can be achieved on heating; however, the corresponding hydrated halides of \(\mathrm{Be}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg}\) suffer hydrolysis on heating.

Hydrated chlorides of \(\mathrm{Be}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg}\) suffer hydrolysis on heating.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q49 - Solubility of BeSO4 and MgSO4 vs BaSO4

questiontext.text: Why are \(\mathrm{BeSO}_4\) and \(\mathrm{MgSO}_4\) readily soluble in water, whereas the solubility decreases sharply down Group 2 to \(\mathrm{BaSO}_4\)?

Solubility depends on the competition between lattice enthalpy and hydration enthalpy.

However, the greater hydration enthalpies of \(\mathrm{Be}^{2+}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\) overcome the lattice enthalpy factor, making \(\mathrm{BeSO}_4\) and \(\mathrm{MgSO}_4\) readily soluble. As hydration enthalpy decreases down the group, solubility decreases from \(\mathrm{CaSO}_4\) to \(\mathrm{BaSO}_4\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The high hydration enthalpies of \(\mathrm{Be}^{2+}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\) overcome the lattice enthalpy, and decreasing hydration enthalpy down the group reduces solubility.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q50 - Thermal stability of alkaline earth metal carbonates

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q53 - Slaking of lime and formation of sodalime

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q54 - High-temperature reactions of CaO with acidic oxides

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q55 - Reaction of milk of lime with chlorine

questiontext.text: When chlorine (\(\mathrm{Cl}_2\)) reacts with milk of lime (\(\mathrm{Ca(OH)}_2\)), which constituent of bleaching powder is formed along with \(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\)?

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q56 - Avoiding excess CO2 in CaCO3 preparation

questiontext.text: In the preparation of calcium carbonate (\(\mathrm{CaCO}_3\)) by passing carbon dioxide through slaked lime, why should excess \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) be avoided?

Passing \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) through \(\mathrm{Ca(OH)}_2\) precipitates insoluble \(\mathrm{CaCO}_3\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q58 - Temperature for Plaster of Paris vs dead burnt plaster

Bone is continuously solubilised and redeposited (about \(400\text{ mg}\) per day in humans), with all this calcium passing through the blood plasma.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q62 - Stoichiometric mass of CaO from CaCO3 decomposition

questiontext.text: Calcium carbonate (\(\mathrm{CaCO}_3\), molar mass \(= 100\text{ g mol}^{-1}\)) decomposes completely at \(1200\text{ K}\) to give calcium oxide (\(\mathrm{CaO}\), molar mass \(= 56\text{ g mol}^{-1}\)) and \(\mathrm{CO}_2\). What mass of \(\mathrm{CaO}\) is obtained from \(200\text{ g}\) of pure \(\mathrm{CaCO}_3\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of \(\mathrm{CaCO}_3 = 200\text{ g}\); molar mass of \(\mathrm{CaCO}_3 = 100\text{ g mol}^{-1}\); molar mass of \(\mathrm{CaO} = 56\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Relevant Formula
Assuming complete thermal decomposition at \(1200\text{ K}\) with \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) removed:
\[\mathrm{CaCO}_3 \xrightarrow{1200\text{ K}} \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO}_2\]
\(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{CaCO}_3\) yields \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{CaO}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Moles of \(\mathrm{CaCO}_3 = \frac{200\text{ g}}{100\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 2\text{ mol}\).
Moles of \(\mathrm{CaO}\) formed \(= 2\text{ mol}\).
Mass of \(\mathrm{CaO} = 2\text{ mol} \times 56\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 112\text{ g}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
By conservation of mass, \(200\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{CaCO}_3\) gives \(112\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{CaO}\) and \(88\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) (\(112 + 88 = 200\text{ g}\)). The mass of \(\mathrm{CaO}\) obtained is \(112\text{ g}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_SBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q63 - Moles of O2 and H2O2 from KO2 hydrolysis

questiontext.text: When \(4\text{ moles}\) of \(\mathrm{KO}_2\) react completely with excess water, how many moles of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) and \(\mathrm{O}_2\) are produced, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Moles of \(\mathrm{KO}_2 = 4\text{ mol}\); water is in excess.

Step 2: Relevant Chemical Equation
\[2\mathrm{KO}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{KOH} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 + \mathrm{O}_2\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
From the balanced equation, \(2\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{KO}_2\) produces \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) and \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{O}_2\).
Therefore, \(4\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{KO}_2\) produces:
Moles of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 = \frac{4}{2} \times 1 = 2\text{ mol}\).
Moles of \(\mathrm{O}_2 = \frac{4}{2} \times 1 = 2\text{ mol}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The stoichiometric ratio of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2 : \mathrm{O}_2\) is \(1:1\). Thus, \(2\text{ moles}\) of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}_2\) and \(2\text{ moles}\) of \(\mathrm{O}_2\) are produced.

Masses in a typical \(70\text{ kg}\) adult:

Calcium accounts for the bulk of this mass (\(1200\text{ g}\)), and the sum of all four s-block metals is \(1485\text{ g}\).
